title: This was one of my most anticipated shows of the season - oh well! #b...
transcript: In Daniel Radcliffe's new Broadway show, he interacts with tons of audience members, running around the house beforehand selecting people to step in as various other characters with elements of improvisation. This is a revival of Every Brilliant Thing, an interactive solo show by Jonny Donahoe and Duncan Mcmillan. The protagonist tells the story of his mother's multiple attempts to take her own life, which inspires him to create this enormous list of all the little and big things that make life worth living. The hook of that premise, combined with the novelty of audience interaction and the inherently loaded subject matter, gave the show a natural magnetism that was hard to resist. And there were definitely times when it resonated with me pretty strongly, but on the whole, it didn't land the emotional punch that I expected it to. And there's a few potential reasons why. The first kinda obvious thing here is that it's designed for very small, intimate theatres, not Broadway. Even from where I was sitting in, like, center orchestra, I didn't feel far away necessarily, but I also didn't feel part of the fabric of this collaborative process the way that I imagine audiences in smaller spaces would have felt, even maybe when they themselves weren't selected for audience participation. And that dynamic is essentially part of the text. It's part of the dramaturgical backbone of how the show is conceived. So without that, the short run time and narrative simplicity leave the show feeling kind of slight and a bit toothless. But some of that might also be the direction more than the size of the theatre. Compared to the pro-shot on HBO of the original off Broadway production, (which I watched afterwards) it seemed like the director, Jeremy Herrin, really ramped up the bells and whistles, putting even more emphasis on the sense of fun interactivity. And of course, there's a sense of fun built into the premise, but it seems to me that it was intended to feel like a cathartic reprieve from the dark themes, a reminder that the alone are rarely truly alone. But here it felt almost more like a distraction, like keys jingling in front of the audience members to sell them on an otherwise depressing show. Also, while I cannot stress enough how much I like Daniel Radcliffe and how fun it was to have him run by me in the aisles, I wonder if the mere fact of having a celebrity in this role is contributing to that key- jangling effect. His performance on its own terms is really strong in a lot of ways; his personable charm and charisma are on full display, with just the right touch of dramatic pathos to land squarely in the sweet spot of his talent. But I also wonder if the way that he played it, or maybe the way he was directed, also contributed to that lack of emotional bite. He captures this aching, plaintive sincerity in the heavier moments, but I believed that he felt deeply *for* this character, more than I believed him *as* this character. Like there wasn't the deep-seated disquiet that would compel someone to undertake a project like this. Because as charming as this list of brilliant things is, I guess, it's also kind of desperate and unhinged. And without that darker underbelly, the premise can come across a little too cutesy for its own good.
